CoreWeave is one of several companies closely tied to AI infrastructure that are reporting earnings this week. Super Micro Computer Inc, which makes AI servers, also posted its results on Tuesday, giving an outlook that far surpassed estimates. Chip equipment maker Applied Materials Inc delivers its latest numbers on Thursday.

Last month, Microsoft said its cloud unit grew at the fastest clip in four years and Alphabet Inc’s Google posted better-than-expected cloud revenue with a backlog that grew to US$514 billion. That was up from roughly US$460 billion a quarter earlier.

title: Nvidia partner Hon Hai scores profit beat on AI spending surge
article:
(Aug 12): Hon Hai Precision Industry Co reported a better-than-expected increase in quarterly profit, signalling robust global demand for AI hardware.

Net income for the three months ended in June grew 35% to NT$60 billion, versus the average analyst projection of NT$58.4 billion. The company previously reported a 40% rise in quarterly sales. Revenue in July jumped 54.2% to NT$946.5 billion. Analysts on average are looking for a 32% increase in sales in the current quarter.

“The unprecedented investments in global cloud infrastructure will become the most critical growth driver for Hon Hai over the next few years,” rotating CEO Michael Chiang told analysts on a post-earnings call on Wednesday. Hon Hai expects its AI business to grow further in 2027, he said.

Chiang said that the company is on track to start mass production of Nvidia’s highly-anticipated, next-generation Vera Rubin platform in the current quarter and start shipping in the fourth quarter. His comments echoed Nvidia boss Jensen Huang’s statements refuting speculation of a possible delay in the US company’s product release.

The Taiwanese company’s performance has become a key gauge for global AI demand thanks to its role as a major server production partner for Nvidia Corp, whose chips have become the gold standard for the vast majority of data centres.

See also: Nvidia partner Hon Hai’s sales rise 54% on strong AI demand

Hon Hai, also known as Foxconn, is further benefiting from Apple Inc’s sustained growth in the smartphone market. The Taiwanese company remains the primary iPhone manufacturer with handset assembly facilities in both China and India.

Hon Hai has said that shipments of AI racks are expected to maintain their momentum in the current quarter while demand for information and communications technology products is entering peak season.

During Wednesday’s call, Chiang said that Hon Hai will add research and development and production capacity in California, Texas, Wisconsin and Ohio to help meet demand for localised supplies from major US customers.

See also: CXMT narrows gap with SK Hynix and Samsung in smartphone memory

Alphabet Inc, Meta Platforms Inc, Microsoft Corp and Amazon.com Inc — the four largest players in the data centre race — have pledged nearly US$2.4 trillion in AI-related spending over the coming years. That’s as questions about how to monetise the technology persist alongside warnings about overcapacity and growing corporate debt.

Such fears fuelled a tech stock rout in July. This week, strong earnings and bullish forecasts from server maker Super Micro Computer Inc and AI computing resource provider CoreWeave Inc have helped ease some of the concerns.

title: SK Hynix, Samsung shares gain as report says Temasek to invest
article:
(Aug 12): South Korean chipmakers rallied as risk appetite returned after last month’s rout and traders weighed a local media report that Singapore’s Temasek Holdings Pte Ltd plans to invest in Samsung Electronics Co and SK Hynix Inc.

Shares of the chip duo briefly extended gains to more than 8% after Asia Business Daily reported that the state fund plans to invest directly in the two chipmakers through its internal investment team, and is mulling timing. Samsung ended the day up 6.7% while SK Hynix rose 5.5%. The benchmark Kospi gained 3.7%.

Temasek said in response to queries from Bloomberg News that it did not seek advice from the South Korean government on the timing of investments in either SK Hynix or Samsung, and that it first invested in both companies more than two years ago.

The chipmakers saw a brutal sell-off in July as doubts grew over the pace of rapid AI infrastructure buildout, leading to an unwinding of leveraged positions. The shares have been rebounding recently, amid growing expectations the companies will bolster shareholder returns with buy-backs and more dividends.

“It is a positive confidence signal, but I would not see it as a game changer or the main driver of the Kospi rebound,” said Albert Yong, a managing partner of hedge fund Petra Capital Management, referring to the local report. “Samsung and SK Hynix had become technically oversold despite still-strong fundamentals.”

See also: Nvidia’s show of financial force soothes jittery credit markets

SK Hynix last Friday said it will unveil shareholder-return details in the third quarter. Samsung Electronics is expected to follow suit, with KB Securities Co analysts expecting a more than 10-fold increase in shareholder returns.

The valuations of the memory chipmakers have come down to record low levels following the July rout, when both stocks plunged more than 20%. Samsung and SK Hynix are trading at 4.2 and 3.6 times forward earnings respectively, compared with more than 21 times for the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index of global chip peers.

Global funds added nearly US$2 billion ($2.6 billion) worth of Kospi shares on Wednesday, while retail traders sold.

See also: Crypto boss eyes second act for Malaysia’s US$100 bil Forest City

If confirmed, the investment would signal “strong foreign confidence in South Korea’s AI/memory cycle,” said Ha SeokKeun, the chief investment officer of Eugene Asset Management. It would be one of the drivers supporting a Kospi rebound, he added.

title: StanChart expects Indian tech hub roles to grow as AI expands
article:
(Aug 12): Standard Chartered plc expects rebalancing of its global headcount due to the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) but sees hiring growing in markets such as India, home to its largest global capability centres.

“Even if I look at India — our largest GCC (global capability centre) — we predict that our headcount in these markets is only going to grow as we are doing more and more sophisticated work out of our shared service centres, including in India,” group chief operating officer Tanuj Kapilashrami told Bloomberg TV’s Paul Allen on Wednesday.

The British lender employs about 22,000 at its so-called global capability centres in India, which support the bank’s operations worldwide, Kapilashrami said. The firm’s current total global workforce is just over 81,000, with about 50,000 staff trained on AI.

Kapilashrami took over as the group COO in May this year and has over two decades of experience in the global financial services sector. Prior to Standard Chartered, she was with HSBC Holdings plc.

India has emerged as a key hub for GCCs as global firms tap its deep pool of technology, engineering and financial-services talent, making the centres a mission-critical cog of global finance. While low-end jobs have been shifting to places such as the Philippines, sprawling campuses in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Gurugram and Mumbai house armies of quants, risk analysts, investment and tech staff. India’s growing AI capabilities are further cementing its role as a centre for banks seeking to develop and deploy AI across their operations.

Standard Chartered is focused on putting guardrails around AI adoption as it scales the technology across its staff, said Kapilashrami.

See also: Rakuten earns first profit in six years with fintech boost

The bank said in May it plans to eliminate close to 8,000 support roles over the next four years, one of the first global lenders to set out how it expects AI to trim headcount.

Global banks are increasingly using AI to automate routine processes, detect fraud and sharpen lending decisions, while also exploring generative AI for customer service and internal operations.

Standard Chartered is employing more AI-native talent, said Kapilashrami. The lender is already seeing productivity gains from AI adoption and an improvement in its cost-to-income ratio, she added.
